title: ⭐ Practice: three remarks and a fenced phrase

questions.prompt: A club secretary is writing one sentence about Mr Chaabane and wants to add, inside that sentence, that he is the tutor of the course. Where does the addition go, and how is it punctuated?

options.text: immediately before the name Mr Chaabane, with a comma behind it but not in front
immediately after the name Mr Chaabane, with a comma before it and a comma after it
immediately after the name Mr Chaabane, with a comma in front of it but not behind it
at the very end of the sentence, with a comma in front of it but not behind it

questions.explanation: An explanation is fixed to the noun it explains, so it stands the moment that noun has been said — and it is fenced, before and after, because the sentence has to be able to close the gap again. A fence with one post is the commonest fault of all: the reader is told an explanation has begun and never told where it ends. Sending the phrase to the end of the sentence hands it to whatever noun happens to be standing there, which may well be the course rather than the man. And putting it in front of the name explains something the reader has not yet met.

questions.prompt: Four words from this lesson name four different things, and they are easy to confuse because all four belong to the same page. Match each word with what it names.

options.text: e-learning
a cyber student
a time commitment
flexibility
hours of a week promised to one thing, and so to nothing else
the freedom to choose the hour and the place of the studying
learning that is carried to the learner by electronic means
the person who is following a course in that way

questions.explanation: Sort them by what kind of thing each one is and the four come apart at once. One is a method — teaching carried down a wire instead of across a room. One is a person, the human being at the far end of that wire. One is a quantity: hours of a week signed away, which is why it is called a commitment and not a wish. And one is a freedom, and a freedom about two things only, the hour and the place. Notice that the method and the person are not interchangeable, however close their names look, and that the quantity and the freedom pull in opposite directions: one says how much the course will take, the other says only when and where you will give it.

questions.prompt: Under three remarks about studying online, a textbook prints a single line: the remarks were made by e-learners and taken from a magazine for learners of English, in June 2003. What does that line settle?

options.text: that the three remarks agree with one another, since they were printed on a single page
nothing worth having, since only the words of the remarks themselves carry any meaning
who was speaking and when, so that the three remarks stand as opinions held at a known date
that the three remarks are true, since a magazine would not have printed them otherwise

questions.explanation: An attribution names a speaker and a date, and that is its whole business. Knowing that learners said these things, and said them in 2003, tells you what kind of person held the view and how old the view is — and it leaves the view itself entirely open to argument, which is precisely why the book asks you next whether you agree. A magazine prints what its readers write, not what it has checked. Being printed together makes three remarks neighbours, not allies, and on this page two of them pull against the third. And an unsigned, undated sentence is the weakest thing on any page: strip the line away and you cannot even say whose opinion you are reading.

questions.prompt: One learner says that somebody who has not got enough time can make more of it, and the one example the book prints is sleeping less. A class is asked to add examples of its own. Which suggestion does the same work as the printed one?

options.text: hoping that the days will feel longer once the course has begun
counting up the hours that the whole course is going to need
waiting for a term in which there will be much less to do
dropping the long telephone call that fills up every evening

questions.explanation: The printed example works because sleep is not spare: it is one of the places the hours already go, and giving some of it up moves them somewhere else at a price the learner has agreed to pay. Dropping the long evening telephone call does just that: an hour that had a destination now has a different one. Hoping moves nothing. Counting is useful, and it is measurement, not manufacture: at the end of it the learner knows the size of his problem and has not touched it. And waiting for a quieter term postpones the whole question to a week that has not arrived. A real suggestion always names two things, the hours and the place they used to go.

questions.prompt: A rule says that the phrase held between two commas gives additional information about the noun in front of it. A pupil asks what additional means here. Which reply fits the rule?

options.text: that the sentence is complete without the phrase, and stays complete when it goes
that the sentence is incomplete without it, and collapses when it goes
that the sentence means the opposite without it, the phrase carrying the denial
that the sentence cannot be written at all without it, a noun always needing an explanation

questions.explanation: Something added to a finished thing can be taken off again and leave the thing finished, and that is the whole force of the word in the rule: fence the phrase out and a whole sentence must remain. That is also the test to run whenever you are unsure whether your commas belong. A phrase the sentence cannot stand without is not an addition at all but part of the structure, and fencing it would break the line. A phrase that reverses the meaning is doing far more than adding, and no comma announces that. And nouns get along perfectly well unexplained: most of the nouns on this page have no phrase after them whatever.

questions.prompt: In a letter about studying at a distance a pupil writes: nobody keeps me to a timetable, and I have already let two whole weeks go by without opening the course. Is that sentence naming a benefit or a drawback, and why?

options.text: a benefit: it shows the pupil is honest about himself, which every argument needs
a drawback: the freedom it names is exactly what allowed the work to stop
a benefit: the freedom it names is exactly what lets a learner work at his own pace
neither: it reports what the pupil did and takes no side about the method itself

questions.explanation: Read the two halves together and the sentence convicts the thing it describes. The freedom is real — and the pupil has just told you what it cost him, two weeks in which nothing whatever happened, because nothing outside him required anything. Working at one's own pace is the same freedom seen on a week when the work got done, and that is not the week being reported here. Taking no side is impossible once a loss has been named. And honesty makes an argument believable without making its content good news: a candid account of a fortnight lost is still an account of a fortnight lost.
